'''Cadambur Tiruvenkatachari Rajagopal''' (8 September 1903 &ndash; 25 April 1978) was an Indian [[mathematician]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=C T Rajagopal - Biography |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Rajagopal/ |access-date=2024-07-02 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>

==Biography==
Rajagopal was born in [[Triplicane]], Madras, India. He was the first son of Tiruvenkatachari and Padmammal. He had two younger brothers, [[C.T. Venugopal]], a distinguished civil servant, and [[C. T. K. Chari]]. They also had a young sister, Kamala. He studied at [[Presidency College, Chennai|Presidency College]] and graduated with an Honours in mathematics in 1925. He was involved in the clerical service and then taught mathematics at [[Annamalai University]]. Rajagopal taught mathematics at [[Madras Christian College]] from 1931 to 1951. He joined the [[Ramanujan Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics]] in 1951.<ref name=":0" />

Collaborating on the teaching of [[conic section]]s, Rajagopal and Vaniyambadi Rajagopala Srinivasaraghavan wrote a [[textbook]], ''An Introduction to Analytical Conics'', that was published in 1955 by [[Oxford University Press]] in India. A reviewer noted "a pleasing feature is the frequent reference to the history of the subject", and "the authors pursue the theory in great detail, proving a large number of subsidiary results."<ref>E.J.F. Primrose (1957) "Review: ''An introduction to analytical conics'' by Rajagopal & Srinivasaraghvan", [[The Mathematical Gazette]] 41 {{doi|10.2307/3610142}}</ref>

Rajagopal became director of the [[Ramanujan Institute for Advanced Study in Mathematics]] in 1955.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imsc.res.in/~rao/ramanujan/newnow/riasm.htm|title=RIASM History}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://ddd.uab.cat/pub/fsunyercor/fsunyercor_556.pdf|title=Letter from C.T.Rajagopal as Head of RIASM}}</ref> He helped the Institute to become India's leading mathematics research centre. The Institute<ref>{{cite web|title=RIASM merges with UM|url=http://www.chennaibest.com/cityresources/education/institutes1.asp#raman}}</ref> is now associated with the [[University of Madras]], after it was merged with the Department of Mathematics at the university in 1967.{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

Rajagopal conducted research on sequences, series, summability, and published more than 80 papers but is most noted for his work in the area of generalising and unifying [[Abelian and tauberian theorems|Tauberian theorems]]. He also did research in many other mathematical topics.{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

Rajagopal also conducted research in the history of medieval Indian mathematics. He showed that the series for arctan x discovered by [[James Gregory (mathematician)|James Gregory]] and those for sin x and cos x discovered by [[Isaac Newton]] were known to the Hindu mathematicians 150 years earlier. He identified [[Madhava of Sangamagrama|Madhava]] as the first discoverer of these series.{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

==Works==

* 1949: (with M.S. Rangachari) "A Neglected Chapter of Hindu Mathematics", [[Scripta Mathematica]] 15: 201–9
* 1951: (with M.S. Rangachari) "On the Hindu proof of Gregory's series", ''Scripta Mathematica'' 17: 65–74.
* 1949: (with A. Venkataraman) "The sine and cosine [[power series]] in Hindu mathematics", ''Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal (Science)'' 15: 1–13.
* 1955: (with V. R. Srinivasaraghavan) [https://books.google.com/books?id=t38HGQAACAAJ Introduction to Analytical Conics] via [[Google Books]]
* 1977/8: (with M. S. Rangachari) "An Untapped Source of Medieval Keralese Mathematics", ''Archive for History of Exact Sciences'' 18(2): 89–102.
* 1986: (with M.S Rangachari) "On Medieval Kerala Mathematics" [[Archive for History of Exact Sciences]] 35: 91–99 {{doi|10.1007/BF00357622}}
